sol-audit.intent: Audit this Solidity contract for reentrancy and access-control issues: pragma solidity ^0.8.20; contract TipJar { mapping(address=>uint) public bal; function deposit() external payable { bal[msg.sender] += msg.value; } function withdraw() external { uint a = bal[msg.sender]; (bool ok,) = msg.sender.call{value: a}(""); require(ok); bal[msg.sender] = 0; } }

output.summary: TipJar has a critical reentrancy flaw: withdraw() sends ETH before zeroing the balance, so an attacker contract can re-enter and drain all deposits. No access-control flaws were found, since each user only touches their own balance.

findings.title: Reentrancy in withdraw() (CEI violation)
findings.rationale: bal[msg.sender] is zeroed only after msg.sender.call. A malicious fallback can re-enter withdraw() repeatedly with the same balance and drain all ETH. Zero the balance before the call, or add a ReentrancyGuard.

findings.title: Zero-amount withdrawals allowed
findings.rationale: withdraw() runs with a balance of 0, making a useless external call to arbitrary code and wasting gas. Add require(a > 0).

findings.title: Bare require without error message
findings.rationale: require(ok) gives no revert reason, which makes failed withdrawals hard to debug. Use a custom error, e.g. TransferFailed().

findings.title: No events emitted
findings.rationale: deposit() and withdraw() emit no events, which hinders off-chain monitoring, indexing and incident response. Emit Deposit and Withdrawal events.

findings.title: Access control: none required, no emergency controls
findings.rationale: Per-user balances need no owner checks, which is correct. However, there is no pause or circuit breaker to stop withdrawals if an exploit is detected. Consider Pausable if appropriate.

findings.title: Forced ETH is unaccounted
findings.rationale: ETH sent via selfdestruct or coinbase bypasses deposit() and is permanently locked. Do not rely on address(this).balance equaling the sum of bal.
